problem: Source says the questions were demanded 'confusedly on all hands'; 'confusedly' is dropped.
new_text: I had thrown on some clothes, though horror shook every limb. I came out of my room. The sleepers were all awake: cries of alarm and terrified murmurs sounded in every room. Door after door was flung open; one person looked out, then another; the gallery filled. Gentlemen and ladies alike had left their beds, and "Oh! What is it?" "Who is hurt?" "What has happened?" "Fetch a light!" "Is it fire?" "Are there robbers?" "Where shall we run?" was demanded in confusion on all sides. Without the moonlight they would have been in total darkness. They ran back and forth; they crowded together; some sobbed, some stumbled. The confusion was hopeless.

new_text: No: stillness returned. Every murmur and movement gradually ceased, and within about an hour Thornfield Hall was as hushed as a desert. It seemed that sleep and night had resumed their rule. Meanwhile the moon sank; she was about to set. Not wanting to sit in the cold and darkness, I thought I would lie on my bed, dressed as I was. I left the window and crossed the carpet quietly; as I stooped to take off my shoes, a cautious hand tapped softly at the door.

new_text: Here, then, I was on the third floor, locked into one of its mysterious rooms; night around me; a pale and bloody spectacle under my eyes and hands; a murderess separated from me by no more than a single door. Yes—that was the truly terrifying part—the rest I could endure. But I shuddered at the thought of Grace Poole bursting in on me.

problem: Source 'so tame under the violence or treachery done him' — 'or treachery' is dropped.
new_text: And this man I bent over—this commonplace, quiet stranger—how had he become entangled in the web of horror? And why had the Fury attacked him? What brought him to this part of the house at such an hour, when he should have been asleep in bed? I had heard Mr. Rochester assign him a room below—what drew him here? And why, now, was he so meek under the violence or treachery done to him? Why did he submit so quietly to the secrecy Mr. Rochester imposed? Why did Mr. Rochester impose it? His guest had been savaged, his own life had been plotted against on a previous occasion; and both attacks he smothered in secrecy and buried in silence! Finally, I could see that Mason was submissive to Mr. Rochester; that the latter's forceful will held complete power over the former's passivity. The few words they had exchanged confirmed this. It was obvious that in their history together, the passive nature of the one had always been ruled by the active energy of the other. Where, then, had Mr. Rochester's terror come from when he heard of Mason's arrival? Why had the mere name of this unresisting man—whom a single word now sufficed to control like a child—struck him, a few hours ago, as a thunderbolt strikes an oak?

new_text: "Not at all!—courage! Two weeks from now you'll scarcely be the worse for it. You've lost a little blood, that's all. Carter, tell him there's no danger."

problem: Source 'all the yard was quiet' becomes 'The yard was empty', a different (stronger) claim.
new_text: It was by now half past five, and the sun was about to rise; but I found the kitchen still dark and quiet. The side door was fastened; I opened it as silently as I could. The whole yard was quiet, but the gates stood wide open, and a post-chaise with horses harnessed and the driver on the box waited just outside. I went to him and said the gentlemen were coming; he nodded. Then I looked carefully around and listened. The stillness of early morning held everything; the curtains were still drawn over the servants' windows; small birds were just beginning to chirp in the blossoming orchard trees, whose branches drooped like white garlands over the wall on one side of the yard; the carriage horses stamped now and then in their stalls. All else was quiet.

problem: Source 'happiness in pleasure—I mean in heartless, sensual pleasure' is rendered 'mindless, shallow pleasure', dropping Rochester's confession of sensuality; also 'shedding of blood' narrowed to 'murder'.
new_text: "Well then, Jane, use your imagination. Suppose you were no longer a well-brought-up, disciplined young woman, but a wild boy spoiled from childhood. Imagine yourself in a remote foreign country. Imagine that there you commit a grave error—never mind what kind or from what motive—but one whose consequences must follow you through life and poison your whole existence. Mind, I don't say a crime; I am not speaking of bloodshed or any guilty act that would bring the law down on you. My word is error. The consequences of what you have done become, in time, utterly unbearable. You take steps to find relief—unusual steps, but neither unlawful nor wicked. Still you are miserable; for hope has left you at the very edge of life. Your noon sun darkens in an eclipse that you feel will last until it sets. Bitter and degrading memories become the only food of your mind. You wander here and there, seeking rest in exile—happiness in pleasure, I mean in heartless, sensual pleasure, the kind that dulls the mind and deadens the heart. Weary in heart and withered in soul, you come home after years of self-imposed exile. You meet someone new—how or where doesn't matter. In this stranger you find the good and bright qualities you have sought for twenty years and never found before; and they are all fresh, healthy, unspoiled and unstained. Such company revives you, regenerates you. You feel better days returning—higher hopes, purer feelings. You want to begin your life again, to spend your remaining days in a way more worthy of an immortal being. To achieve this end, are you justified in leaping over a barrier of custom—a mere conventional obstacle that neither your conscience approves nor your judgment supports?"
